articles.title: Does the Quran Confirm the Bible It Contradicts? The Islamic Dilemma Examined
articles.excerpt: The argument says the Quran traps itself by affirming scriptures it contradicts. It works only if the Quran says two things it never says.
articles.content:
The argument has become a fixture of online debate. The Quran affirms the Torah and the Gospel as revelation from God. Those scriptures contradict the Quran on the crucifixion, the divinity of Jesus and much else. So either the scriptures are reliable, in which case the Quran is wrong, or they are corrupt, in which case the Quran was wrong to affirm them. Christian debaters call this "the Islamic Dilemma" and present it as a closed trap. It deserves a close reading, because its force depends on two premises that the Quran does not supply.

Premise one: that the Injīl is the New Testament

The Quran speaks of the Tawrāt (the Torah), given to Moses, and the Injīl (the Gospel, from the Greek euangelion), given to Jesus. The grammar is consistent throughout. The Injīl is something God gave to Jesus.

وَقَفَّيْنَا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِم بِعِيسَى ٱبْنِ مَرْيَمَ مُصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ ۖ وَءَاتَيْنَٰهُ ٱلْإِنجِيلَ فِيهِ هُدًۭى وَنُورٌۭ وَمُصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةِ وَهُدًۭى وَمَوْعِظَةًۭ لِّلْمُتَّقِينَ ﴿٤٦﴾
"We sent Jesus son of Mary in their footsteps, confirming the Torah that came before him, and We gave him the Gospel, in which is guidance and light, confirming the Torah before it, as guidance and admonition for the God-conscious."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:46

The four canonical Gospels are a different kind of document. They are narratives about Jesus, written in Greek by later authors, and they bear the names that church tradition attached to them. Much of their content consists of what others said and did around Jesus, including accounts of his death that the Quran denies.

The dilemma therefore needs an equation the Quran never makes: the Injīl of the Quran equals the four Gospels of the later Christian canon. Once that equation is dropped, the first horn loses its object. The Quran affirms a revelation given to a prophet. The critic supplies a library compiled by his followers and assigns the affirmation to it.

Premise two: that 5:43 and 5:47 certify an intact text

The verses most often cited are these two. The first concerns Jews of Medina who brought a legal case to the Prophet.

وَكَيْفَ يُحَكِّمُونَكَ وَعِندَهُمُ ٱلتَّوْرَىٰةُ فِيهَا حُكْمُ ٱللَّهِ ثُمَّ يَتَوَلَّوْنَ مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ ۚ وَمَآ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ بِٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ ﴿٤٣﴾
"How is it that they come to you for judgment when they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God, and then turn away after that? Those are not believers."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:43

The verse makes a specific claim: the Torah held in Medina contained God's judgment on the matter in dispute. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī preserves the case itself. A Jewish man and woman had committed adultery. The Prophet asked what the Torah prescribed. The men who brought the case said public shaming and flogging, and when the scroll was opened, one of them covered the verse of stoning with his hand.

مَا تَجِدُونَ فِي التَّوْرَاةِ فِي شَأْنِ الرَّجْمِ
"What do you find in the Torah concerning stoning?"
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3635

The report cuts both ways against the dilemma. God's ruling was present in the text, which is exactly what 5:43 asserts. And the custodians of the text were concealing it, which is exactly what the Quran elsewhere calls taḥrīf (distortion). The Hebrew Bible does prescribe death for adultery, so the ruling survived. The episode describes a scripture that retained divine content while its holders obscured it.

Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:47 follows the same logic. It tells the people of the Injīl to judge by what God revealed in it. An instruction to judge by what God revealed in a book presupposes that divine content remains recoverable. It makes no claim that every sentence in the book is divine.

The same chapter records the distortion

The critic's reading of 5:43 and 5:47 has to set aside a verse thirty verses earlier in the same chapter.

فَبِمَا نَقْضِهِم مِّيثَٰقَهُمْ لَعَنَّٰهُمْ وَجَعَلْنَا قُلُوبَهُمْ قَٰسِيَةًۭ ۖ يُحَرِّفُونَ ٱلْكَلِمَ عَن مَّوَاضِعِهِۦ ۙ وَنَسُوا۟ حَظًّۭا مِّمَّا ذُكِّرُوا۟ بِهِۦ ﴿١٣﴾
"Because they broke their covenant, We cursed them and hardened their hearts. They distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:13

Two charges sit side by side here. Words were moved from their proper places, and a portion of the original message was forgotten. Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:79 condemns those who write a book with their own hands and then say it is from God. Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:78 describes a party who twist their tongues with the scripture so that listeners take their words for scripture.

Classical exegetes debated whether this alteration touched the wording, the meaning, or both. None of them read 5:47 as a certificate of textual perfection, because the text of al-Māʾidah itself forbids that reading. The dilemma gets its contradiction by quoting half of one chapter against the other half.

Sūrat al-Māʾidah on the earlier scripture
VerseWhat it saysWhat it establishes
5:13The people of the covenant "distort words from their places" and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded ofAlteration and loss
5:43The Torah held in Medina contains "the judgment of God"Divine content survives
5:46God gave Jesus the Injīl, confirming the Torah before itThe Injīl is a revelation given to Jesus
5:47The people of the Injīl are to judge by what God revealed in itDivine content remains recoverable
5:48The Quran confirms the earlier scripture and is muhaymin (guardian) over itThe Quran is the criterion

Muhaymin: the Quran's own model

The Quran states its relationship to earlier scripture in one word, in the verse that immediately follows 5:47.

وَأَنزَلْنَآ إِلَيْكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ بِٱلْحَقِّ مُصَدِّقًۭا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ وَمُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ ﴿٤٨﴾
"We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming the scripture that came before it and as a guardian over it."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:48

Muhaymin (guardian, overseer, the one who stands witness over something) carries the sense of an authority that checks and verifies. A guardian over a text confirms what in it is sound and identifies what is not. The verse pairs taṣdīq (confirmation) with haymanah (oversight), and the pairing only makes sense if the earlier text contains both.

This is the position the dilemma leaves out. Its two horns are total reliability and total corruption. The Quran asserts a third position: earlier revelation survives in the scriptures of the Jews and Christians, mixed with human additions and losses, and the final revelation is the criterion by which the two are told apart.

[ce_diagram id="islamic-dilemma-three-positions"]The dilemma offers two options. The Quran, in 5:48, takes a third.[/ce_diagram]

Sūrat Yūnus 10:94, which tells the Prophet to ask those who read the scripture before him if he is in doubt, fits the same model. A witness asked about the pattern of prophecy must retain knowledge of it. The verse says nothing about the textual condition of what the witness reads.

What the Bible's own record shows

The Quranic account of partial alteration matches what the Bible and its textual critics report. The prophet Jeremiah rebuked those who claimed to possess the law of the Lord, and said that the false pen of the scribes had made it into a lie (Jeremiah 8:8). That is a biblical prophet accusing scribes of corrupting scripture within the Bible's own pages.

The New Testament shows the same process in its manuscripts. The last twelve verses of Mark (16:9 to 20) are absent from the two oldest complete Greek manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and many modern translations bracket them or flag them in a note. Christian textual scholarship reconstructs an earlier text precisely because the transmitted text grew over time. The Quran described that process in the seventh century.

[ce_figure id="codex-sinaiticus-mark-ending"]Codex Sinaiticus, 4th century. The Gospel of Mark ends at 16:8, "for they were afraid," and the closing title Euangelion kata Markon (Gospel according to Mark) follows. Verses 9 to 20 are absent.[/ce_figure]

Revelation 22:18 and the closed canon

A related argument holds that the Bible forbids any later revelation, citing the warning at the end of the book of Revelation against anyone who adds to its words (Revelation 22:18 to 19). The warning concerns "the words of the prophecy of this book," the Apocalypse of John.

Deuteronomy carries the same warning in almost identical terms: do not add to the word I command you, and do not take from it (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). Christians accept that Joshua, the Psalms, the Prophets and the entire New Testament came after that warning without violating it. The same reasoning applies to Revelation. Its place as the last book of a bound Bible is an arrangement made by later compilers; its author could not have been sealing a collection that did not yet exist as one volume.

What remains of the dilemma

The argument needs the Quran to say two things. It needs the Injīl to be the four Gospels, and it needs 5:43 to 5:47 to certify a complete and unaltered text. The Quran says neither. It describes a revelation given to Jesus, a scripture that still carried divine rulings in Medina, a record of distortion and forgetting in the same chapter, and a final revelation appointed as guardian over the whole.

That position is internally consistent, and it is the position the historical evidence supports. The dilemma presents two options because it has removed the third, and the third is the one the Quran holds.

articles.title: Do Quran 9:5 and 9:29 Command War on All Non-Muslims?
articles.excerpt: Critics call 9:5 the "verse of the sword" and read 9:29 as a standing order to fight unbelief. The surrounding verses set out who was to be fought, and why.
articles.content:
Two verses from Sūrat al-Tawbah carry most of the weight in the argument that Islam cannot coexist with anyone else. The first, 9:5, is often called āyat al-sayf (the verse of the sword). The second, 9:29, commands fighting certain People of the Book until they pay the jizyah (a tax on non-Muslim subjects of a Muslim state). Critics read both as permanent commands to wage war on unbelief as such. The verses have a context, and the context sits in the same chapter, often in the very next line.

[ce_figure id="qundusi-quran-tawbah"]A page of Sūrat al-Tawbah (9:93) from a Quran copied in the Maghribi Qundusi script by Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Qundusi, 19th century.[/ce_figure]

Who the polytheists of 9:5 were

Sūrat al-Tawbah opens with a declaration of disassociation from the Arabian polytheists with whom the Muslims held treaties, and grants them four months of free movement (9:1 to 2). Before the command in 9:5 comes an exception.

إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ عَٰهَدتُّم مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَنقُصُوكُمْ شَيْـًۭٔا وَلَمْ يُظَٰهِرُوا۟ عَلَيْكُمْ أَحَدًۭا فَأَتِمُّوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِمْ عَهْدَهُمْ إِلَىٰ مُدَّتِهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُتَّقِينَ ﴿٤﴾
"Excepted are those polytheists with whom you made a treaty and who have not failed you in anything, nor supported anyone against you. Fulfil your treaty with them to the end of its term. God loves the God-conscious."
Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:4

Then the command itself.

فَإِذَا ٱنسَلَخَ ٱلْأَشْهُرُ ٱلْحُرُمُ فَٱقْتُلُوا۟ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ وَخُذُوهُمْ وَٱحْصُرُوهُمْ وَٱقْعُدُوا۟ لَهُمْ كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍۢ ۚ فَإِن تَابُوا۟ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتَوُا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ فَخَلُّوا۟ سَبِيلَهُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ ﴿٥﴾
"When the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, seize them, besiege them, and wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish prayer and give zakāh, let them go their way. God is Forgiving, Merciful."
Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:5

The subject of the verse is a defined group: polytheists who had broken their treaties, as distinct from those in 9:4 who had kept theirs. Nine verses later the chapter states the grievance in plain terms.

أَلَا تُقَٰتِلُونَ قَوْمًۭا نَّكَثُوٓا۟ أَيْمَٰنَهُمْ وَهَمُّوا۟ بِإِخْرَاجِ ٱلرَّسُولِ وَهُم بَدَءُوكُمْ أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ ۚ أَتَخْشَوْنَهُمْ ۚ فَٱللَّهُ أَحَقُّ أَن تَخْشَوْهُ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ ﴿١٣﴾
"Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, resolved to drive out the Messenger, and began hostilities against you first? Do you fear them? God has more right to be feared, if you are believers."
Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:13

The reasons given are broken oaths, a plan to expel the Prophet, and aggression initiated by the other side. Those are the conditions of a war already under way. The language of 9:5, including "wherever you find them," describes the conduct of that war once the grace period ended.

The verse that follows

The strongest evidence against the reading of 9:5 as a command to kill unbelievers for their unbelief is 9:6.

وَإِنْ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ ٱسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ حَتَّىٰ يَسْمَعَ كَلَٰمَ ٱللَّهِ ثُمَّ أَبْلِغْهُ مَأْمَنَهُۥ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ قَوْمٌۭ لَّا يَعْلَمُونَ ﴿٦﴾
"If any of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant it, so that he may hear the word of God. Then escort him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know."
Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:6

A polytheist who asks for protection receives it, hears the message, and is then conveyed to safety while still a polytheist. The verse requires no conversion as the price of his life. A command to exterminate unbelief could not coexist with a command to escort unbelievers home under armed protection. The juxtaposition shows that the target of 9:5 was hostility, and the belief of the enemy did not decide his fate.

Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:1 to 9:13 in order
VersesWhat they say
9:1 to 2Disassociation from the polytheists who held treaties with the Muslims, with four months of free movement
9:4Exception: those who kept their treaty and supported no one against the Muslims. "Fulfil your treaty with them to the end of its term."
9:5After the sacred months, the command against the treaty-breakers; "if they repent … let them go their way"
9:6A polytheist who seeks protection receives it, hears the word of God, and is escorted to safety
9:13The grievance: they "broke their oaths, resolved to drive out the Messenger, and began hostilities against you first"

Jizyah and the terms of 9:29

قَٰتِلُوا۟ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَلَا بِٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلْءَاخِرِ وَلَا يُحَرِّمُونَ مَا حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُۥ وَلَا يَدِينُونَ دِينَ ٱلْحَقِّ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ حَتَّىٰ يُعْطُوا۟ ٱلْجِزْيَةَ عَن يَدٍۢ وَهُمْ صَٰغِرُونَ ﴿٢٩﴾
"Fight those among the people who were given the Book who do not believe in God or the Last Day, who do not forbid what God and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not follow the religion of truth, until they pay the jizyah from their hand, subdued."
Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:29

Al-Ṭabarī records, on the authority of the early exegete Mujāhid, that the verse came down when the Prophet was commanded to fight the Byzantine Romans, after which the Tabūk expedition set out. The verse belongs to a confrontation between the Medinan state and an imperial power on its northern border.

The end point of the fighting is the most telling detail. The verse sets the payment of a tax as the condition that ends hostilities. A community that pays the jizyah keeps its houses of worship and its religious law. A war that ends in a tax paid by people who remain Jews and Christians is by its own terms a war about political authority. Conversion appears nowhere in the verse as a condition.

The exegetes differed over ṣāghirūn (subdued, brought low). Ibn Kathīr gave the word a harsh sense of humiliation. Al-Ṭabarī records several views, among them the view that the act of paying is itself the submission the verse means. Historians describe the institution in practice as a tax levied in lieu of military service. Under the second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the Christian Jarājimah tribe was exempted when it agreed to serve in the army, and the poor, the elderly, women and clergy generally paid nothing. Rulers also abused the system in some periods, collecting it even from converts to fill the treasury. The abuse contradicts the rule, and the rule is what the verse establishes.

The general rule in the Quran

The Quran states the principle that governs relations with non-Muslims who are not at war with the Muslims.

لَّا يَنْهَىٰكُمُ ٱللَّهُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقَٰتِلُوكُمْ فِى ٱلدِّينِ وَلَمْ يُخْرِجُوكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِكُمْ أَن تَبَرُّوهُمْ وَتُقْسِطُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُقْسِطِينَ ﴿٨﴾
"God does not forbid you from dealing kindly and justly with those who have not fought you because of your religion and have not driven you from your homes. God loves those who are just."
Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah 60:8
إِنَّمَا يَنْهَىٰكُمُ ٱللَّهُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ قَٰتَلُوكُمْ فِى ٱلدِّينِ وَأَخْرَجُوكُم مِّن دِيَٰرِكُمْ وَظَٰهَرُوا۟ عَلَىٰٓ إِخْرَاجِكُمْ أَن تَوَلَّوْهُمْ ۚ وَمَن يَتَوَلَّهُمْ فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلظَّٰلِمُونَ ﴿٩﴾
"God only forbids you from taking as allies those who fought you because of your religion, drove you from your homes and helped to drive you out. Whoever takes them as allies, those are the wrongdoers."
Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah 60:9

The line falls between those who fight and those who do not. Fighting is permitted against "those who fight you," with transgression forbidden (2:190). When the enemy inclines to peace, the believers must incline to it too (8:61). And 2:256 declares that there is no compulsion in religion. The verses of al-Tawbah apply this rule to a particular war; they do not repeal it.

The abrogation argument

Some classical jurists held that 9:5 abrogated the earlier verses of restraint and turned a specific command into a general one. Critics and militants rely on that position alike. It was one juristic position among several, and it runs into the text it claims to interpret: the exceptions of 9:4, the protection of 9:6 and the stated grievances of 9:13 all remain in the Quran. A reading of 9:5 that makes those verses dead letters has abandoned the chapter to make its case. The site's article on Meccan and Medinan revelation and abrogation treats the wider question.

Read in the order the chapter gives them, 9:5 and 9:29 describe a war against treaty-breakers and a hostile empire, with conditions for ending it that leave the religion of the defeated intact.

articles.title: Is Islam a Religion of Peace? What the Terrorism Data Shows
articles.excerpt: Critics cite tens of thousands of "Islamic terror attacks" and polls of Muslim opinion. The numbers are real, and they say something different from what is claimed.
articles.content:
The charge usually arrives with a number attached. One ex-Muslim commentator told an American audience that more than 72,000 Islamic terrorist attacks have struck almost every country on earth since 9/11, and attributed the figure to a well-known annual terrorism index. A popular video essay cites polling to estimate 150 million Islamists and three million potential terrorists. The numbers deserve scrutiny, because the argument stands or falls with them. So does the honest answer: jihadist groups are among the deadliest organisations operating today, and Muslims have to reckon with that.

[ce_figure id="pexels-12944080"]A mosque at dawn.[/ce_figure]

Where the 72,000 figure comes from

The index cited is published annually by the Institute for Economics & Peace. Its underlying database records a little over 76,000 terrorist incidents of every kind, worldwide, for the whole period from 2007 to 2025. That total covers terrorism of every ideology. A count of 72,000 attacks by one religious category since 2001 cannot come from that dataset.

The figure matches a running tally kept by an anti-Islam website that counts any killing where the perpetrator saw Islam as a motive, "as interpreted by the perpetrator," and whose own compilers say the list includes honour killings and executions alongside terrorism. A partisan tally with its own inclusion rules is a different thing from a research index, and attributing one to the other misleads the audience.

What the index reports

The 2026 edition of the index reports that deaths from terrorism fell 28 percent in 2025 to 5,582, the lowest figure since 2007. The Islamic State and its affiliates remained the deadliest organisation, responsible for 17 percent of attacks worldwide. The Sahel region of Africa accounted for over half of all terrorism deaths.

Two findings complicate the critics' story. Fatalities in the West rose to 57 in 2025, and the report attributes the rise largely to antisemitism, Islamophobia and political terrorism. And in sub-Saharan Africa, where jihadist violence is heaviest, 71 percent of recruits named abuses by state security forces as the final trigger for joining an armed group. The data describes an insurgency feeding on failed states and ungoverned borders, carried out under a religious banner.

Who dies

The United States National Counterterrorism Center reported in 2011 that, where the religious affiliation of victims could be determined, Muslims suffered between 82 and 97 percent of terrorism-related deaths over the previous five years. The same report attributed roughly 70 percent of the year's 12,533 terrorism deaths to Sunni extremist groups. Both facts stand together. Jihadist groups kill more people than any other category of terrorist, and the people they kill are overwhelmingly Muslims.

That second fact matters for the argument. If Islam itself produced the violence, the victims would be the enemies Islam names. The actual victims are overwhelmingly Muslim villagers and worshippers. Groups that massacre Muslims at prayer are waging war on the Muslim community as much as on anyone.

The figures behind the charge
MeasureFigureSource
Terrorist incidents of every ideology, worldwide, 2007 to 2025a little over 76,000Institute for Economics & Peace
Deaths from terrorism in 20255,582 (down 28 percent; lowest since 2007)Global Terrorism Index 2026
Share of attacks by the Islamic State and affiliates17 percentGlobal Terrorism Index 2026
Fatalities in the West in 202557Global Terrorism Index 2026
Share of terrorism deaths suffered by Muslims, where victims' religion was known82 to 97 percentUS National Counterterrorism Center, 2011

What Muslims say about violence

A 2013 Pew Research Center survey of eleven Muslim publics asked whether suicide bombing and other violence against civilians could be justified in defence of Islam. In Pakistan 89 percent said never; in Indonesia 81 percent; in Nigeria 78 percent. In Malaysia 58 percent said never, while 27 percent said such attacks were sometimes or often justified. Among Palestinian Muslims a majority said such attacks could be justified. The results show broad rejection of terrorism alongside troubling minorities in specific countries, most of them in active conflicts.

[ce_diagram id="pew-2013-never-justified"]Muslims who said suicide bombing and other violence against civilians in defence of Islam is never justified, in the four countries named above. Pew Research Center, 2013.[/ce_diagram]

The polling figures cited for stoning and the death penalty for apostasy come from a companion Pew survey, and they measure something else. They are shares of Muslims who already favour making sharia the official law of their country, and they record opinions about state legal punishment. A person can hold a harsh view of criminal law and reject terrorism. Pakistani Muslims, who returned high support for classical punishments in one survey, returned 89 percent rejection of attacks on civilians in the other. Treating one set of numbers as a count of potential terrorists conflates two questions the surveys kept apart.

What the sources forbid

The Quran lists the unlawful killing of a human being among the gravest prohibitions.

وَلَا تَقْتُلُوا۟ ٱلنَّفْسَ ٱلَّتِى حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَّا بِٱلْحَقِّ ۚ ذَٰلِكُمْ وَصَّىٰكُم بِهِۦ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ ﴿١٥١﴾
"Do not kill the soul God has made sacred, except by right. This He has enjoined upon you so that you may reason."
Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:151

The Prophet forbade the killing of women and children in war (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3015). He also placed the non-Muslim living under a covenant of safety beyond the reach of any Muslim's violence.

مَنْ قَتَلَ مُعَاهَدًا لَمْ يَرَحْ رَائِحَةَ الْجَنَّةِ، وَإِنَّ رِيحَهَا تُوجَدُ مِنْ مَسِيرَةِ أَرْبَعِينَ عَامًا
"Whoever kills a person under a covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise, though its fragrance can be found from a distance of forty years."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3166

A muʿāhad (one under covenant) is a non-Muslim who lives among Muslims or enters their lands under an agreement of safety. The modern visa and the grant of citizenship are covenants of exactly this kind. A Muslim who lives in London or Paris lives under exactly such a covenant with the people around him. The attacker who kills them breaks the covenant and, on the Prophet's own words, forfeits Paradise.

Islam and Islamism

The same video essay that estimates three million potential terrorists draws a distinction between Islam and Islamism, and concedes that hundreds of millions of Muslims are not Islamists. Its own example is Egypt, where millions of Muslims took to the streets in 2013 against the Muslim Brotherhood government. The distinction is sound, and it defeats the claim that the violence flows from the religion as such. Movements such as the Islamic State and al-Qaeda are modern political projects that emerged from the wreckage of states in the last half century, and Muslims have been their first and most numerous opponents.

The honest position holds two things at once. Jihadist violence is real, organised and deadly, and it claims Islamic justification. The Quran and the Prophet forbid what it does, the data shows Muslims are its main victims, and the surveys show most Muslims reject it. A religion whose texts forbid killing the covenanted, and whose adherents are the chief victims and chief opponents of the groups that do it, is poorly described by the figures its critics repeat.

articles.title: Does the Quran Teach Muslims to Hate Jews?
articles.excerpt: A British Muslim says he was born to hate Jews. Critics say the Quran taught him. The texts, and the Prophet's own conduct, tell a different story.
articles.content:
Kasim Hafeez grew up in a devout Muslim family in England and later described himself as born to hate Jews. He named the sources of that hatred: speakers in mosques and schools through the 1990s, a university culture in which hostility to Israel was a badge of honour, and a narrative in which Jews were occupiers and the West their instrument. His hatred ended when he read the other side of the argument and then travelled to see the country for himself. Critics use stories like his as evidence that Islam breeds antisemitism. The story, as he tells it, is about political indoctrination. The question is whether the Quran supplies what the indoctrination claimed.

"Do not take them as allies"

۞ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تَتَّخِذُوا۟ ٱلْيَهُودَ وَٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰٓ أَوْلِيَآءَ ۘ بَعْضُهُمْ أَوْلِيَآءُ بَعْضٍۢ ۚ وَمَن يَتَوَلَّهُم مِّنكُمْ فَإِنَّهُۥ مِنْهُمْ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهْدِى ٱلْقَوْمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ ﴿٥١﴾
"O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies. They are allies of one another. Whoever among you takes them as allies is one of them. God does not guide the wrongdoing people."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:51

The key word is awliyāʾ (allies, protectors, patrons). It belongs to the vocabulary of political and military alliance, and the verse was addressed to a Medinan community surrounded by hostile coalitions, some of whose members, the next verse says, hastened toward the other side for fear of misfortune (5:52). Sūrat al-Mumtaḥanah draws the line explicitly: kindness and justice toward those who do not fight Muslims, and no alliance with those who do (60:8 to 9).

The decisive evidence comes from a verse in the same chapter, which permits Muslim men to marry Jewish and Christian women.

ٱلْيَوْمَ أُحِلَّ لَكُمُ ٱلطَّيِّبَٰتُ ۖ وَطَعَامُ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ حِلٌّۭ لَّكُمْ وَطَعَامُكُمْ حِلٌّۭ لَّهُمْ ۖ وَٱلْمُحْصَنَٰتُ مِنَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنَٰتِ وَٱلْمُحْصَنَٰتُ مِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ مِن قَبْلِكُمْ ﴿٥﴾
"Today all good things have been made lawful for you. The food of those given the Book is lawful for you, and your food is lawful for them. So too are chaste women from the believers and chaste women from those given the Book before you."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:5

Marriage in the Quran is defined by mawaddah (love) and raḥmah (mercy) placed between the spouses (30:21). A scripture that commanded Muslims to hate Jews could not also invite a Muslim to build a home with a Jewish wife, share her table and raise children with her. Sūrat al-Māʾidah does both in the same chapter because 5:51 concerns political allegiance in time of conflict.

"The worst of creatures"

إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ وَٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ فِى نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ خَٰلِدِينَ فِيهَآ ۚ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمْ شَرُّ ٱلْبَرِيَّةِ ﴿٦﴾
"Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book and the polytheists will be in the fire of Hell, abiding in it forever. They are the worst of creatures."
Sūrat al-Bayyinah 98:6

The verse describes a specific group, "those who disbelieve among" the People of the Book. The same chapter defines them by what they rejected: they divided only after the clear proof came to them (98:4). The judgement falls on rejection of truth once recognised. A Jew as such is not its subject.

The Quran says so directly elsewhere.

۞ لَيْسُوا۟ سَوَآءًۭ ۗ مِّنْ أَهْلِ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ أُمَّةٌۭ قَآئِمَةٌۭ يَتْلُونَ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ ءَانَآءَ ٱلَّيْلِ وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ ﴿١١٣﴾
"They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of God through the night and prostrate."
Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:113
يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلْيَوْمِ ٱلْءَاخِرِ وَيَأْمُرُونَ بِٱلْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ ٱلْمُنكَرِ وَيُسَٰرِعُونَ فِى ٱلْخَيْرَٰتِ وَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ ﴿١١٤﴾
"They believe in God and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong and hasten to good deeds. They are among the righteous."
Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:114

Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:69 promises that Jews and Christians who believe in God and the Last Day and do good need have no fear. A text that names some Jews among the righteous cannot be read as a verdict on Jews as a people.

"Be apes, despised"

Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:65 recalls a punishment: those who broke the Sabbath were told to become apes. Sūrat al-Aʿrāf 7:163 identifies them as the people of one town by the sea who devised a trick to fish on the Sabbath. The account concerns one community's violation of its covenant, told as a warning to believers who might do the same. The same book says of the Children of Israel that God gave them the Book, judgement and prophethood and "preferred them above the worlds" (45:16; also 2:47). Modern polemicists who turn the Sabbath-breakers into a slur for all Jews have done something the Quran never does.

The hadith of the stone and the tree

لاَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تُقَاتِلُوا الْيَهُودَ حَتَّى يَقُولَ الْحَجَرُ وَرَاءَهُ الْيَهُودِيُّ يَا مُسْلِمُ، هَذَا يَهُودِيٌّ وَرَائِي فَاقْتُلْهُ
"The Hour will not come until you fight the Jews, and the stone behind which a Jew is hiding says, "O Muslim, here is a Jew behind me, so kill him.""
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2926

The report is authentic, and its form determines its meaning. It opens "the Hour will not come until," the formula of prophecies about the end of time, and it describes stones that speak. It foretells a battle in the final events before the Day of Judgement. Nothing in it commands Muslims to seek out or harm any Jew living now. The rules that govern how Muslims treat Jews today come from texts addressed to the present, such as 60:8, which commands justice and kindness toward all who do not fight Muslims.

How the Prophet treated Jews

The Prophet's own conduct shows what these texts meant in daily life. When a funeral procession passed and he stood, his companions told him it was the bier of a Jew.

أَلَيْسَتْ نَفْسًا
"Is it not a soul?"
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1312

A Jewish boy served in his household, and when the boy fell ill the Prophet went to visit him (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1356). At his death his armour was held in pledge by a Jew against thirty measures of barley (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2916). The man whose example Muslims are commanded to follow stood in respect for a Jewish dead man and died in a relationship of commercial trust with a Jewish creditor.

[ce_figure id="medina-1880"]Medina about 1880, photographed by an Ottoman officer. The Prophet's Mosque stands behind the city walls.[/ce_figure]

The Quran did record conflict. Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:82 says the believers would find the Jews and the polytheists most intense in hostility toward them, and the Christians nearest in affection. The verse reports the posture of particular communities toward the early Muslims in Arabia, and it legislates nothing.

The texts cited and what they address
TextWhat it addresses
5:51Awliyāʾ (allies): political and military alliance, addressed to a Medinan community surrounded by hostile coalitions
5:5The food of the People of the Book is lawful to Muslims, and Muslim men may marry their chaste women
98:6Those who rejected the truth after the clear proof came to them (98:4)
3:113 to 114"They are not all alike": an upright community among the People of the Book, counted among the righteous
2:65; 7:163The Sabbath-breakers of one town by the sea
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 2926A prophecy of a battle among the final events before the Day of Judgement

Politics and hatred

A Muslim can hold strong views about the policies of any state, including Israel, and remain bound by the Quran's rule on enmity.

يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ لِلَّهِ شُهَدَآءَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ ۖ وَلَا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ شَنَـَٔانُ قَوْمٍ عَلَىٰٓ أَلَّا تَعْدِلُوا۟ ۚ ٱعْدِلُوا۟ هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ ۖ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ خَبِيرٌۢ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ ﴿٨﴾
"O you who believe, stand firm for God as witnesses to justice, and do not let hatred of a people lead you to be unjust. Be just: that is closer to God-consciousness. Fear God; God is aware of what you do."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:8

The verse assumes that Muslims will sometimes feel hostility toward a people, and forbids that hostility from corrupting their judgement. Hafeez describes a youth in which grievance became hatred and hatred became a plan to join a training camp. By his own account that path ran through sermons and campus politics. The Quran commanded the opposite of what he was taught: to stand for justice when hostility is at its strongest.

articles.title: Does Quran 4:34 Permit a Husband to Beat His Wife?
articles.excerpt: The verse contains a word that means "strike." What the Prophet, his companions and the classical jurists did with that word is the rest of the story.
articles.content:
No verse of the Quran is quoted more often in arguments about women than Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:34. Its final instruction contains the verb ḍaraba (to strike), and critics read it as divine licence for domestic violence. An honest answer has to begin by admitting that the word is there. It then has to ask what the verse addresses, what sequence it lays down, and what limits the Prophet and the earliest authorities attached to it.

[ce_figure id="pexels-13456843"]Two hands, wedding rings.[/ce_figure]
ٱلرِّجَالُ قَوَّٰمُونَ عَلَى ٱلنِّسَآءِ بِمَا فَضَّلَ ٱللَّهُ بَعْضَهُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍۢ وَبِمَآ أَنفَقُوا۟ مِنْ أَمْوَٰلِهِمْ ۚ فَٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ قَٰنِتَٰتٌ حَٰفِظَٰتٌۭ لِّلْغَيْبِ بِمَا حَفِظَ ٱللَّهُ ۚ وَٱلَّٰتِى تَخَافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ فَعِظُوهُنَّ وَٱهْجُرُوهُنَّ فِى ٱلْمَضَاجِعِ وَٱضْرِبُوهُنَّ ۖ فَإِنْ أَطَعْنَكُمْ فَلَا تَبْغُوا۟ عَلَيْهِنَّ سَبِيلًا ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيًّۭا كَبِيرًۭا ﴿٣٤﴾
"Men are maintainers of women, by what God has given some over others and by what they spend from their wealth. Righteous women are devout, guarding in absence what God would have them guard. As for those from whom you fear nushūz, admonish them, then leave them alone in bed, then strike them. If they obey you, seek no way against them. God is Most High, Most Great."
Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:34

What nushūz means

The verse concerns nushūz, from a root meaning to rise up. The word names a serious breach of the marital bond, more than ordinary disagreement or disobedience in daily matters. The Prophet identified the kind of breach in view in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage.

فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ فِي النِّسَاءِ فَإِنَّكُمْ أَخَذْتُمُوهُنَّ بِأَمَانِ اللَّهِ وَاسْتَحْلَلْتُمْ فُرُوجَهُنَّ بِكَلِمَةِ اللَّهِ وَلَكُمْ عَلَيْهِنَّ أَنْ لاَ يُوطِئْنَ فُرُشَكُمْ أَحَدًا تَكْرَهُونَهُ ‏.‏ فَإِنْ فَعَلْنَ ذَلِكَ فَاضْرِبُوهُنَّ ضَرْبًا غَيْرَ مُبَرِّحٍ
"Fear God concerning women. You have taken them on the trust of God. Your right over them is that they do not admit into your homes anyone you dislike. If they do that, you may strike them in a way that is not severe."
Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1218

The Quran applies the same word to husbands. Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:128 addresses the wife who fears nushūz from her husband, and directs the couple toward a negotiated settlement, "and settlement is best." Either spouse can breach the bond. The verse under discussion addresses one form of that breach.

A sequence aimed at reconciliation

The verse sets out three steps in order: counsel, then withdrawal from the marriage bed, then the final measure. The very next verse moves the dispute out of the husband's hands.

وَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ شِقَاقَ بَيْنِهِمَا فَٱبْعَثُوا۟ حَكَمًۭا مِّنْ أَهْلِهِۦ وَحَكَمًۭا مِّنْ أَهْلِهَآ إِن يُرِيدَآ إِصْلَٰحًۭا يُوَفِّقِ ٱللَّهُ بَيْنَهُمَآ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيمًا خَبِيرًۭا ﴿٣٥﴾
"If you fear a rift between the two, appoint an arbiter from his family and an arbiter from hers. If they want reconciliation, God will bring it about between them. God is All-Knowing, All-Aware."
Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:35

Read together, 4:34 and 4:35 describe a staged process for saving a marriage in crisis, with arbitration by both families as the next stage. The verse closes with a prohibition: once the breach ends, the husband may "seek no way against" his wife. Retaliation and further pressure are both ruled out.

[ce_diagram id="nisa-4-34-stages"]The sequence of 4:34 and 4:35, with the limit the Prophet and the earliest authorities set on the third stage.[/ce_diagram]

What the earliest authorities permitted

The Prophet limited the act in the sermon quoted above with the phrase ghayr mubarriḥ (not severe, not causing harm). The earliest exegetes asked what that meant. Al-Ṭabarī records in his commentary on this verse that ʿAṭāʾ asked Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet's cousin and the foremost early interpreter of the Quran, what a strike that is not severe would be. Ibn ʿAbbās answered: with the siwāk (the small twig used to clean the teeth) or something like it.

Ibn Kathīr reports the same limit from Ibn ʿAbbās and others, and cites al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's explanation that the strike must leave no mark. He adds that the jurists defined it as one that breaks no limb and leaves no trace. The Prophet separately forbade striking the face (Sunan Abī Dāwūd 2142). What the classical tradition permitted, at its outer limit, was a symbolic gesture of displeasure, and any act that caused injury fell outside the permission altogether.

What the Prophet did

The Prophet's own practice goes further than the rule. His wife ʿĀʾishah reported that he never struck a woman or a servant with his hand (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2328). When he first forbade men to strike their wives, ʿUmar complained that wives had grown bold, and the Prophet allowed it. Women then came to his household in numbers to complain of their husbands.

لَقَدْ طَافَ بِآلِ مُحَمَّدٍ نِسَاءٌ كَثِيرٌ يَشْكُونَ أَزْوَاجَهُنَّ لَيْسَ أُولَئِكَ بِخِيَارِكُمْ
"Many women have come to the family of Muhammad complaining about their husbands. Those men are not the best of you."
Sunan Abī Dāwūd 2146
خَيْرُكُمْ خَيْرُكُمْ لأَهْلِهِ وَأَنَا خَيْرُكُمْ لأَهْلِي
"The best of you is the best to his family, and I am the best of you to my family."
Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 3895

The permission stood, and the Prophet declared that the men who used it were not the best of the community. He never used it himself. In Islamic ethics that combination has a clear meaning: an act can be legally permitted and still be the conduct of lesser men, and the believer is told to imitate the best.

The frame around the verse

The Quran defines marriage by the mawaddah (love) and raḥmah (mercy) God places between spouses (30:21). It forbids a husband to keep his wife "to harm her" and calls whoever does so a wrongdoer against himself (2:231). Domestic abuse violates both texts, the Prophet's limit of ghayr mubarriḥ and his personal example at the same time. A man who injures his wife and cites 4:34 has cited a verse whose own authorities condemn what he did.

The critic is right that the word is in the verse. The tradition that received it spent its first generation narrowing it to a twig, and the man who delivered it never raised his hand to a woman in his life.

articles.title: Is Allah a Slave-Master or a God of Love?
articles.excerpt: An ex-Muslim turned Christian says Islam knows only a tyrant who threatens his slaves. The Quran speaks of a God who loves, and says so by name.
articles.content:
The charge comes most sharply from former Muslims who have become Christians. In Christianity, the argument runs, God is a father who loves his people and makes promises to them. In Islam, God is a tyrannical slave-master who commands and threatens, and a religion built on an abusive relationship produces abusive people. One such speaker told an interviewer that Muslims are "abused" by their religion from birth. The charge makes claims about the Quran that can be checked, and a psychological claim that deserves the same scrutiny.

[ce_figure id="al-wadud-calligraphy"]Al-Wadūd (the Loving), one of the names of God, in Arabic calligraphy.[/ce_figure]

The Loving is one of God's names

The Quran names God al-Wadūd (the Loving, the Affectionate).

وَهُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلْوَدُودُ ﴿١٤﴾
"And He is the Forgiving, the Loving."
Sūrat al-Burūj 85:14

The name appears again in Sūrat Hūd 11:90, paired with mercy. The verb of love runs throughout the text: God loves those who do good (2:195), those who keep their commitments (3:76), those who act justly (60:8). The relationship runs both ways. Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:54 describes a people "whom He loves and who love Him," and Sūrat Maryam 19:96 promises that the Most Merciful will create wudd (love) for those who believe and do good.

The Quran does not call God "Father." Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ declares that He neither begets nor was begotten (112:3), and the Quran guards that boundary carefully because it separates the Creator from the created. The refusal of the paternal title protects God's transcendence. The love it expresses in other language is explicit and repeated.

Love in the Quran
VerseWhat it says
85:14"He is the Forgiving, the Loving"
11:90Al-Wadūd (the Loving), paired with mercy
2:195God loves those who do good
3:76God loves those who keep their commitments
60:8God loves those who act justly
5:54A people "whom He loves and who love Him"
19:96The Most Merciful will create wudd (love) for those who believe and do good

Mercy greater than a mother's

When the critic contrasts a fatherly God with a tyrant, the Prophet's own image answers him. Captives were brought to Medina, and among them a woman searching for her child. When she found him she clutched him to her and nursed him.

اللَّهُ أَرْحَمُ بِعِبَادِهِ مِنْ هَذِهِ بِوَلَدِهَا
"God is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5999

The Prophet also taught that God divided mercy into a hundred parts, kept ninety-nine with Himself and sent one into the world, and that from this single part every creature shows tenderness to its young (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6000). God wrote upon Himself that His mercy prevails over His wrath (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7404). The Quran states the same principle as a divine decree.

قُل لِّمَن مَّا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۖ قُل لِّلَّهِ ۚ كَتَبَ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ ﴿١٢﴾
"Say: To whom belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God. He has prescribed mercy upon Himself."
Sūrat al-Anʿām 6:12

A God who runs toward His servant

An abusive master waits to punish. The God of the Quran and the Prophet's teaching moves toward the one who turns to Him faster than that person moves toward God.

وَإِنْ تَقَرَّبَ إِلَىَّ بِشِبْرٍ تَقَرَّبْتُ إِلَيْهِ ذِرَاعًا، وَإِنْ تَقَرَّبَ إِلَىَّ ذِرَاعًا تَقَرَّبْتُ إِلَيْهِ بَاعًا، وَإِنْ أَتَانِي يَمْشِي أَتَيْتُهُ هَرْوَلَةً
"If he draws near to Me by a hand-span, I draw near to him by an arm's length. If he draws near to Me by an arm's length, I draw near to him by the span of outstretched arms. If he comes to Me walking, I come to him running."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 7405
وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِى عَنِّى فَإِنِّى قَرِيبٌ ۖ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ ٱلدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ ۖ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا۟ لِى وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا۟ بِى لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ ﴿١٨٦﴾
"When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that they may be rightly guided."
Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:186
۞ قُلْ يَٰعِبَادِىَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا۟ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا۟ مِن رَّحْمَةِ ٱللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا ۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ ﴿٥٣﴾
"Say: O My servants who have wronged themselves, do not despair of the mercy of God. God forgives all sins. He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
Sūrat al-Zumar 39:53

The last verse addresses people who have sinned against themselves, and calls them "My servants" in the same breath. The possessive expresses belonging. A tyrant's slaves are property; these servants are called back by name after their worst failures.

Servanthood and freedom

The word the critic finds so offensive is ʿabd (servant, worshipper). In the Quranic view every human being serves something: wealth, status, appetite, a ruler, the approval of others. Servanthood to God, who needs nothing from His creatures, releases a person from servitude to all of these. The same Quran that calls believers servants of God tells them that God has honoured every child of Adam (17:70). A master who honours his servants above much of creation and runs toward them when they approach bears little resemblance to the tyrant of the charge.

Hell in both traditions

The critic points to the Quran's descriptions of hell, including the replacement of burnt skin in 4:56, as proof of a sadistic God. A Christian making this argument faces his own scripture. Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew sends the cursed "into the eternal fire" (Matthew 25:41) and says they "will go away into eternal punishment" (Matthew 25:46). Mark describes a place "where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched" (Mark 9:48). The Quran and the Gospels both teach that rejecting God has eternal consequences. If warnings of hell make a religion abusive, the charge falls on Christianity by the same measure.

The site treats the justice of eternal punishment in its articles on hellfire and on finite sins and infinite punishment. The point here is narrower: the critic has chosen a standard his own faith cannot meet.

The psychological claim

The argument ends with a diagnosis: hurt people hurt people, Islam hurts Muslims, so Muslims hurt others. The speaker offered no evidence for the first link beyond the claim itself. The polling data discussed in the site's article on terrorism shows large majorities of Muslims rejecting violence against civilians, which is hard to square with a population formed by abuse. A religion whose scripture opens nearly every chapter with the names of God "the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," and whose adherents recite those names in every unit of prayer, forms its people around mercy by the plain count of their daily words.

articles.title: Does Islam Teach That Paradise Is Earned by Works?
articles.excerpt: A popular Christian explainer says Muslims try to earn Paradise through the Five Pillars, and that even Muhammad was unsure of his fate. The Prophet said the opposite.
articles.content:
A widely viewed Christian explainer summarises Islam this way: a Muslim's entrance into Paradise hinges on obedience to the Five Pillars, Allah may still reject him, and even Muhammad was not sure whether he would be admitted. The contrast it draws is between Islamic salvation by works and Christian salvation by grace. The summary gets the Islamic position wrong on its central point, and the Prophet corrected the same misunderstanding in his own lifetime.

[ce_figure id="pexels-7031844"]Stairs rising toward the light.[/ce_figure]

No one enters Paradise by his deeds

لَنْ يُنَجِّيَ أَحَدًا مِنْكُمْ عَمَلُهُ
"The deeds of none of you will save him."
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6463

His companions asked whether this applied even to him. He answered that it did, "unless God covers me with His mercy," and then told them to do good deeds with sincerity and moderation. The same report holds both elements together. Deeds are commanded, and deeds do not purchase salvation. Entry into Paradise is an act of divine mercy toward people whose faith and effort God accepts.

The Quran describes Paradise in the same terms.

سَابِقُوٓا۟ إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍۢ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ وَجَنَّةٍ عَرْضُهَا كَعَرْضِ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ أُعِدَّتْ لِلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَرُسُلِهِۦ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ فَضْلُ ٱللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشَآءُ ۚ وَٱللَّهُ ذُو ٱلْفَضْلِ ٱلْعَظِيمِ ﴿٢١﴾
"Race toward forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for those who believe in God and His messengers. That is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills. God is the possessor of great bounty."
Sūrat al-Ḥadīd 57:21

The key word is faḍl (bounty, unearned favour). Paradise is prepared for believers and granted as a gift. A wage is owed; a gift is given. The Quran places Paradise in the second category.

"I do not know what will be done with me"

قُلْ مَا كُنتُ بِدْعًۭا مِّنَ ٱلرُّسُلِ وَمَآ أَدْرِى مَا يُفْعَلُ بِى وَلَا بِكُمْ ۖ إِنْ أَتَّبِعُ إِلَّا مَا يُوحَىٰٓ إِلَىَّ وَمَآ أَنَا۠ إِلَّا نَذِيرٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ ﴿٩﴾
"Say: I am no novelty among the messengers, and I do not know what will be done with me or with you. I only follow what is revealed to me, and I am only a clear warner."
Sūrat al-Aḥqāf 46:9

The verse belongs to a Meccan chapter and answers opponents who demanded that the Prophet produce knowledge of the unseen. He disclaims any knowledge of the future beyond what revelation gives him. Revelation later gave him more. After the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiyah, Sūrat al-Fatḥ addressed him directly.

لِّيَغْفِرَ لَكَ ٱللَّهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِن ذَنۢبِكَ وَمَا تَأَخَّرَ وَيُتِمَّ نِعْمَتَهُۥ عَلَيْكَ وَيَهْدِيَكَ صِرَٰطًۭا مُّسْتَقِيمًۭا ﴿٢﴾
"That God may forgive you your past and future faults, complete His favour upon you and guide you on a straight path."
Sūrat al-Fatḥ 48:2

The explainer quotes the earlier verse and omits the later one. Read in sequence, the two verses show a prophet who claimed no certainty on his own authority and then received it from God.

His statement that even he would be saved only by God's mercy expresses the same humility, and it is the humility the Quran asks of every believer. Muslim spirituality holds khawf (fear of falling short) together with rajāʾ (hope in God's mercy). A believer who presumed on salvation would have stopped taking God seriously, and a believer who despaired of it would have disobeyed 39:53, which forbids despair of God's mercy.

The pillars in their place

The Five Pillars are acts of worship and obedience. The testimony of faith, prayer, almsgiving, fasting and pilgrimage (where one is able) structure a Muslim's life around God. Muslims perform them because God commanded them and because they shape the heart. Muslims take them seriously, as the explainer says. Treating them as a payment schedule misreads their purpose. The Prophet's teaching about mercy was given to men who performed every one of these acts, and he told them their deeds would not save them.

Faith and works in the Christian scriptures

The contrast of "grace against works" is itself contested inside Christianity. The Letter of James says that "by works a man is justified, and not only by faith" (James 2:24). Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew says that not everyone who calls him Lord will enter the Kingdom of Heaven, "but he who does the will of my Father" (Matthew 7:21), and in the scene of the final judgement the nations are divided by what they did for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner (Matthew 25:31 to 46). Christian theologians have argued since the Reformation over how these passages relate to justification by faith.

Islam holds a position of its own. Salvation comes by God's mercy, received through faith, and faith shows itself in deeds that God commands and accepts. The Quran joins "those who believe and do righteous deeds" dozens of times. Neither half stands alone, and the pair together purchases nothing.

Deeds and mercy in both scriptures
TextWhat it says
Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6463"The deeds of none of you will save him"
Quran 57:21Paradise is "the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills"
Quran 46:9"I do not know what will be done with me or with you"
James 2:24"By works a man is justified, and not only by faith"
Matthew 7:21Entry to the Kingdom for "he who does the will of my Father"
Matthew 25:31 to 46The nations judged by what they did for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner

What the explainer should have said

An accurate summary of the Islamic teaching would read: Muslims believe Paradise is a gift of God's mercy to those who believe and strive to obey Him; they perform the pillars as worship; they hope for mercy and fear their own failures; and their Prophet taught that no one, himself included, would enter Paradise by deeds alone. That summary leaves the Christian critic with a real theological disagreement to argue about, the question of atonement and the cross. It removes the caricature the argument depended on.

articles.title: Can a Muslim Be a Loyal Citizen of a Western Democracy?
articles.excerpt: Critics say Islam denies human dignity and seeks to conquer the societies that host it. The Quran's teaching on dignity, justice and covenants says otherwise.
articles.content:
The argument has moved from the lecture hall to the campaign stage. Islam, its critics say, is incompatible with Western civilisation. It denies that every human being has equal dignity, it refuses freedom of conscience, and its adherents in the West are the vanguard of an "Islamisation" that will end with sharia replacing the constitution. One ex-Muslim debater put the first point in scriptural terms: the Quran calls unbelievers "the worst of creatures," while the West holds that every person has intrinsic worth. Each claim can be tested against the Quran and against what Western Muslims do.

[ce_figure id="pexels-14631741"]A civic building with its flag.[/ce_figure]

Human dignity

The Quran grounds human dignity in creation, and extends it to every descendant of Adam.

۞ وَلَقَدْ كَرَّمْنَا بَنِىٓ ءَادَمَ وَحَمَلْنَٰهُمْ فِى ٱلْبَرِّ وَٱلْبَحْرِ وَرَزَقْنَٰهُم مِّنَ ٱلطَّيِّبَٰتِ وَفَضَّلْنَٰهُمْ عَلَىٰ كَثِيرٍۢ مِّمَّنْ خَلَقْنَا تَفْضِيلًۭا ﴿٧٠﴾
"We have honoured the children of Adam, carried them on land and sea, provided them with good things and favoured them above much of what We created."
Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:70

The verse uses the widest term available, banī Ādam (the children of Adam). Believer and unbeliever, Muslim and Jew, share the honour because they share the origin.

يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍۢ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلْنَٰكُمْ شُعُوبًۭا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتْقَىٰكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌۭ ﴿١٣﴾
"O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes so that you may know one another. The noblest of you in the sight of God is the most God-conscious. God is All-Knowing, All-Aware."
Sūrat al-Ḥujurāt 49:13

The phrase "worst of creatures" in 98:6 is a judgement on those who rejected the truth after it became clear to them, as the same chapter specifies (98:4), and it concerns their standing before God in the next life. The site's article on the Quran and the Jews examines the verse in detail. A verdict about moral accountability before God leaves the dignity of 17:70 intact, in the same way that Christian teaching on the damnation of the unrepentant leaves the image of God in every person intact.

Equal justice

Equality before the law, the critic says, comes from Christianity and is foreign to Islam. The Quran commands justice with a rigour that reaches past every loyalty a person has.

يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ شُهَدَآءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَوِ ٱلْوَٰلِدَيْنِ وَٱلْأَقْرَبِينَ ۚ إِن يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا أَوْ فَقِيرًۭا فَٱللَّهُ أَوْلَىٰ بِهِمَا ۖ فَلَا تَتَّبِعُوا۟ ٱلْهَوَىٰٓ أَن تَعْدِلُوا۟ ﴿١٣٥﴾
"O you who believe, stand firmly for justice as witnesses for God, even against yourselves, your parents or your relatives, whether the person is rich or poor. God has more right to both. Do not follow desire, lest you swerve from justice."
Sūrat al-Nisāʾ 4:135
يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ لِلَّهِ شُهَدَآءَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ ۖ وَلَا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ شَنَـَٔانُ قَوْمٍ عَلَىٰٓ أَلَّا تَعْدِلُوا۟ ۚ ٱعْدِلُوا۟ هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ ۖ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ خَبِيرٌۢ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ ﴿٨﴾
"O you who believe, stand firm for God as witnesses to justice, and do not let hatred of a people lead you to be unjust. Be just: that is closer to God-consciousness. Fear God; God is aware of what you do."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:8

The first verse overrides kinship and class. The second overrides enmity. Justice owed to one's enemies is the hardest form of equality before the law, and the Quran commands it by name.

Freedom of conscience

Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:256 declares that there is no compulsion in religion. The harder question of apostasy law in Islamic legal history is treated at length in the site's articles on apostasy and freedom and on apostasy in international law. For the question of citizenship, the relevant point is simpler. A Muslim living in a Western democracy is bound by the Quran to respect the religious choices of his neighbours, and by the law of his country to respect them in fact. The two obligations point in the same direction.

The covenant of citizenship

The Quran binds Muslims to the agreements they make.

يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ أَوْفُوا۟ بِٱلْعُقُودِ ﴿١﴾
"O you who believe, fulfil your contracts."
Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:1
وَأَوْفُوا۟ بِٱلْعَهْدِ ۖ إِنَّ ٱلْعَهْدَ كَانَ مَسْـُٔولًۭا ﴿٣٤﴾
"And fulfil every commitment. The commitment will be asked about."
Sūrat al-Isrāʾ 17:34

A Muslim who accepts a visa, residence or citizenship enters an agreement with the society that grants it: to obey its laws and to live peaceably among its people. The Prophet warned that whoever kills a person living under a covenant with the Muslims will not smell the fragrance of Paradise (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3166). The covenant binds in both directions. On the Quran's own terms, a Muslim who enters a Western country and then works to subvert its constitution breaks a promise God commanded him to keep.

Democratic principles and the Quranic texts
PrincipleVersesWhat they say
Human dignity17:70; 49:13God has honoured the children of Adam, and made peoples and tribes "so that you may know one another"
Equal justice4:135; 5:8Stand for justice "even against yourselves," and do not let hatred of a people lead you to be unjust
Freedom of conscience2:256There is no compulsion in religion
Keeping covenants5:1; 17:34"Fulfil your contracts"; "fulfil every commitment"

"Islamisation" and the Brotherhood memorandum

Ayaan Hirsi Ali and others point to a 1991 memorandum written by Mohamed Akram, a member of the Muslim Brotherhood in North America, which spoke of destroying Western civilisation "from within." The document is real and was entered as an exhibit in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism-financing trial. Its standing is disputed: some researchers treat it as a strategic plan, others as one member's proposal that never became policy. Either way it records the ambition of a political movement founded in Egypt in 1928, and it is fair to scrutinise any organisation that shares that ambition.

It cannot stand in for the Muslims of the West. A 2017 Pew Research Center survey found that 92 percent of American Muslims say they are proud to be American, and 89 percent say they are proud to be both Muslim and American. Four in five said they were satisfied with the way things were going in their lives. Those figures describe citizens who have made the covenant and mean to keep it.

Where the real disagreements lie

Some tensions are real. Muslims hold moral positions on sexuality, alcohol and family law that differ from prevailing Western opinion. So do many observant Christians and Jews, and liberal democracies exist precisely to let citizens who disagree on such questions live under one law. A Muslim who votes, pays taxes, obeys the law and argues for his convictions through the ballot is doing exactly what democracy asks of every citizen.

Hirsi Ali closes her story by saying that newcomers who want to become like Americans are welcome. The Quran asks the Muslim newcomer to keep his covenant and to deal justly with people who do not share his faith, every one of them a child of Adam whom God has honoured. On those terms the loyal Muslim citizen is the ordinary case, and the Quran is the reason.
